<reason>Both sides argued at a high level and kept the clash tight. A correctly seized the word "achievable" and pressed a real burden — no Israeli coalition, no unified Palestinian signatory, no year in which both exist — and its "alibi/deniable" line and the Gaza-trauma-scaled-80x point were genuinely damaging. But B set and held the decisive comparative frame: "least-bad" is inherently comparative, so A's own alternative must meet the same achievability test. B's "same door, steeper climb" reframe (any rights-bearing single state still terminates in a national majority accepting minority status, which requires more, not less, consent than a border) was the pivot of the debate, and B reinforced it by turning A's own South Africa analogy (consent was still extracted from the white minority) and by noting Hebron's settlers end up inside the shared legislature under A's plan. A's reply — that equality arrives incrementally and survives losing a decade — is a real asymmetry and was well argued, but A never specified when or how the terminal increment (14 million in one polity) is accepted, and A left B's most damaging charge essentially unanswered: that A's mechanism amounts to welcoming formal annexation and hoping the world prices it, i.e. locking in permanent hierarchy while the motion asks for the least-bad outcome. A5.6 waves at this rather than answering it. On pressure questions, B gave a concrete falsifier and answered the Jerusalem-ring/Hebron/coalition question directly; A's falsifier critique was fair but A offered none of its own, as B pointed out. Execution: A's opening and second rebuttal were both clipped, costing it the payoff of two key speeches; B lost only one. B's stray nonexistent reference id is a minor blemish.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's "same door" turn: holding A's rights-trajectory to A's own achievability standard, showing it ends in a Jewish-Israeli majority yielding sovereignty — so whatever pressure could achieve that would buy partition more cheaply, with hard-core settlers outside the legislature rather than inside it. A's incrementalism reply was plausible but never identified when that terminal consent arrives, and never rebutted B's charge that A's route effectively invites formal annexation.</best_rebuttal>
